system:
You judge a requirements contract. A model interviewed the future users of a service and derived a contract from what they told it. You compare that contract with the reference requirements of the same service.

=== REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS (read-only) ===
BR-01: The service serves several independent operating companies at once. The staff of one operating company can never see or change another operating company's drones, models, sites, charging pads, jobs or flights, or their history.

BR-02: The airspace picture (the corridors between sites, the zones that group them, the prohibited zones and the closures) is one and the same for every company, and every company's staff can see all of it.

BR-03: Every member of staff acts in one of three roles: fleet technician or dispatcher at an operating company, or the airspace desk at the platform company. Each action of the service can be taken only by the role these requirements give it to.

BR-04: The airspace desk cannot see any one company's drones, jobs or flights.

BR-05: A fleet technician can add a drone to their company's fleet, stating its model. For each model the service holds how much it can carry, how far it can fly on a full battery, which sensors it carries, and which charging connector it uses.

BR-06: Each drone has a home site, one of its company's sites.

BR-07: A fleet technician can retire a drone. A retired drone stays in its company's history and is never again given a flight or sent to charge.

BR-08: A fleet technician can take a drone out of service for repair and put it back into service. A drone out of service cannot be given a flight.

BR-09: A fleet technician can set up a charging pad at one of their company's sites, stating its connector type.

BR-10: A charging pad is used only by drones of the company that owns it.

BR-11: A fleet technician can send a drone to charge. The service sends it only to a pad whose connector type is the one the drone's model uses, and refuses otherwise.

BR-12: The service keeps, for each drone, a record of when it was taken out of service, repaired or serviced, and put back, and by whom, so that its company can show a regulator how the drone has been looked after.

BR-13: A dispatcher can record a delivery job: a load to be carried from one site to another.

BR-14: A dispatcher can record an inspection job: the sensors it needs and a list of points to visit in a set order, ending back where it started.

BR-15: A dispatcher plans a flight for a job by choosing the drone and the way, a chain of corridors between named sites.

BR-16: The service never chooses a drone or a way for a flight, and never puts one in place of the dispatcher's choice.

BR-17: On a dispatcher's request, the service shows which of their company's drones could get to where a job starts.

BR-18: A flight leaves only after a dispatcher has signed it off; nothing but a dispatcher's own action signs a flight off.

BR-19: A dispatcher can call off a flight.

BR-20: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose drone cannot do the job: a load heavier than its model can carry, a way longer than its model can fly, or, for an inspection, a sensor the job needs that its model does not carry.

BR-21: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose way passes through a zone where flying is prohibited, or through a closure in force at any time during the flight.

BR-22: The service does not let more drones take off or land at a site at the same time than the site has places for.

BR-23: When dispatchers planning at the same time sign off flights that would use the same drone at overlapping times, only one sign-off succeeds, and the others are told why they failed.

BR-24: When it judges whether a drone can fly a way, the service does not count on the full range of a full battery, since batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.

BR-25: The service accepts reports from people and devices outside the company that a flight's load is ready, that its drone has reached a point of its job, and that it has arrived, and it records each against the flight.

BR-26: A report that arrives more than once is applied once.

BR-27: A report that arrives late or out of order never undoes a later one: a flight's state follows the order in which things happened, not the order in which the reports arrived.

BR-28: When a report a flight is waiting for does not come in time, such as its arrival, the service flags the flight to the dispatchers of its company, since nobody watches every drone.

BR-29: A drone that restarts in flight and carries on stays on the same flight, and its reports after the restart count for that flight.

BR-30: The airspace desk can record the corridors between named sites, the zones that group them, and the zones where the authorities prohibit flying.

BR-31: The airspace desk can enter a planned closure, with a start and an end time, and a sudden closure, which applies at once. It can amend a closure, for example by widening its area or moving its end time, and the amendment applies from the moment it is entered.

BR-32: When a closure is entered or amended, the service tells each company's dispatchers which of their flights it affects, including flights already in the air, and tells no company about another's flights.

BR-33: The service does not itself call off, reroute or change a flight because of a closure; that is the dispatcher's decision.

BR-34: When a closure is entered, the airspace desk sees how much disruption it caused across the customers, as totals that name no company and show no company's flights.

BR-35: The service can be restarted, or crash, while drones are flying, and afterwards carries on from where it was: nothing it had recorded is lost or applied twice.

BR-36: An instruction the service sends to a drone or to charging equipment takes effect once, even when it gets through twice or the service sends it again because it cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.

BR-37: The service tells each company's own systems what happens to that company's drones and jobs, and nothing about any other company's.

BR-38: The service offers no way to steer a drone.
=== END OF REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS ===

The names in the reference that look like `name` stand for these values:
(none)

=== OUT OF SCOPE: things the users said they do not want ===
- Management or analytical reports, exports, and dashboards.
- Login through an external identity provider.
- i18n.
- Compliance with any regulation, or a compliance audit. Regulations are cited as provenance only (`domain-profile.md` §9).
- Data retention and erasure: no retention schedule, deletion on request, or pseudonymisation of history.
- Backups.
- High availability or multi-node deployment.
- User accounts, sign-up, passwords, or user management. Staff identities are issued outside the system; each request carries a signed token (D-23).
- Notifying people by e-mail, text message, or phone. Domain events go only to the event webhook (D-18).
- Route planning or automatic choice of a drone. The system validates the dispatcher's choice and never makes it (D-33).
- Remote piloting or real-time flight control. Flight control is on the drone (`domain-profile.md` §2).
- Weather data or forecasts.
- Billing, invoicing, or pricing of deliveries and inspections.
- Onboarding of new operating companies or management of tenants through the system.
=== TECHNICAL ADDITIONS: never stated by the users, and not counted against a contract ===
- Autoscaling.
- A second-level cache.
- A message broker, queue, or coordinator. Every boundary is HTTP (`domain-profile.md` §3).
- Geometric or geospatial computation. Position is a location or a corridor; coordinates, if present, are descriptive (`domain-profile.md` §4, §6).
- Throughput or latency at the declared scale. Scale is data context (`domain-profile.md` §7); the harness does not apply fleet-scale load during functional gates.
=== END OF LISTS ===

You receive the contract: a list of items, each with an id and a requirement.

For each reference requirement, decide how the contract as a whole covers it:

- covered: the items, together, state every obligation of the requirement — every rule, condition, exception, value and outcome it gives. Wording, order, the words chosen for states and roles, and whether a value is given by its name or by its number do not matter; meaning does.
- partial: the items state at least one of its obligations and leave out at least one other.
- missing: no item states any of its obligations.

An item states an obligation only when it says what the service must do, or must not do, in a case the requirement covers. A general wish, such as that the service be reliable, states none. An item that says the opposite of an obligation does not state it. A requirement that only names another one, or a value another one defines, does not take over that other requirement's obligations.

For each item of the contract, decide its class:

- reference: it states one or more obligations of the reference requirements; name each requirement it states obligations of.
- user_visible: it asks for something on the out-of-scope list.
- technical: it asks for something on the list of technical additions.
- other: none of these — it asks for something no reference requirement asks for, or states nothing checkable.

A contract with no items covers nothing.

Reply with JSON only: an object with two keys. "requirements" is a list with exactly one entry for every reference requirement, in the reference's order; each entry has "id", the requirement's id, "coverage", one of "covered", "partial" or "missing", and "items", the ids of the items that state its obligations (an empty list when it is missing). "items" is a list with exactly one entry for every item of the contract, in the contract's order; each entry has "id", the item's id, "class", one of "reference", "user_visible", "technical" or "other", and "requirements", the ids of the reference requirements it states obligations of (an empty list unless its class is "reference").

The contract has 20 items:

- id: DR-01
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to add new drones to the fleet.
- id: DR-02
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to retire drones from the fleet.
- id: DR-03
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to configure and register charging pads at operational sites.
- id: DR-04
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to instruct a drone to go to a charging pad to charge.
- id: DR-05
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to take a drone out of service for repairs and return it to service once repairs are complete.
- id: DR-06
  requirement: The service must not automatically assign or select a drone for a flight, requiring the selection to be made manually by the dispatcher.
- id: DR-07
  requirement: The service must identify and display to the dispatcher which drones are capable of reaching the starting location of a requested job.
- id: DR-08
  requirement: The service must allow a dispatcher to select the route for a flight along established flight corridors.
- id: DR-09
  requirement: The service must require a dispatcher's sign-off on a planned flight before the drone is permitted to depart.
- id: DR-10
  requirement: The service must allow a dispatcher to call off a flight.
- id: DR-11
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to maintain a shared picture of the airspace, including flight corridors between sites and the zones that group those corridors.
- id: DR-12
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to record planned airspace closures announced by authorities, specifying prohibited flying zones, start times, and end times.
- id: DR-13
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to record sudden airspace closures announced by authorities that take effect immediately.
- id: DR-14
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to amend existing closures during the day, including expanding the closed area and changing the end time.
- id: DR-15
  requirement: When an airspace closure is entered, the service must calculate and present to the airspace desk the total disruption caused across all customer companies without exposing any individual company's proprietary operational details.
- id: DR-16
  requirement: The service must maintain operational isolation between customer companies such that staff of one company or the shared airspace desk cannot inspect an individual company's specific operations.
- id: DR-17
  requirement: The service must identify and handle situations where a planned, sudden, or amended airspace closure takes effect while drones from one or more companies are already in flight within the affected area.
- id: DR-18
  requirement: The service must correctly process incoming status reports from drones even when reports arrive late, out of chronological order, duplicated, or are dropped due to patchy radio coverage.
- id: DR-19
  requirement: The service must ensure instructions transmitted to drones and charging equipment are idempotent, preventing duplicate execution when instructions are resent or duplicated over unreliable communication links.
- id: DR-20
  requirement: The service must persist all drone, flight, and airspace state across application updates, restarts, and server crashes on a single-server deployment without losing track of active flights.
